unit.unitOverview: Research means finding out about a topic or an issue in an organised way, so that you can trust what you learn and explain it to someone else. It is not just typing a question into a phone. Real research means asking the right questions, choosing good sources, gathering information by asking and watching, recording it tidily, and drawing honest conclusions.

explainers.title: Hello and welcome to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This subject is a little different from your other lessons. It is not about learning a long list of facts by heart. Instead, it teaches you a set of thinking skills that you can use for the rest of your life, in every subject and out in the real world.

There are six thinking skills in Global Perspectives, and you will grow all of them, year by year, while you are here:

This whole unit is about the very first skill: Research. It is a wonderful skill to begin with, because you need it before all the others. You cannot analyse, judge or explain a topic well until you have first found out about it. So the work you do here becomes the foundation for everything that follows.

Why does research matter beyond school? Think about the choices grown-ups make every day. A parent choosing the best clinic for a sick child. A shopkeeper deciding which goods will sell. A community leader deciding where to dig a new well. All of them are really doing research: they ask questions, gather information, decide who to trust, and then choose. A learner who practises these skills now will make better decisions for their whole life. That is why we begin here.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you have changed your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in the Ehel Academy way, which means three kinds of support work together:

In the old style of this subject, learners were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'discuss as a class'. In our model, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, treat it as a real conversation. Say your ideas out loud or type them, and let the tutor push your thinking further.

Your research skills will grow in three stages this year, just as a young tree grows. You will begin by starting each skill, then move on to developing it, and finally you will get better at it. Do not worry if something feels tricky at first. Starting is meant to feel like a first try.
bullets: You, at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea, or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were a friendly study partner and a whole class rolled into one. It will discuss your ideas, ask you questions, and give you feedback at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best work, ask the questions that matter most, and get to know the other learners.

explainers.title: Meet Yasmin, our researcher for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one Year 6 learner all the way through the unit. Her name is Yasmin, and she is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

Every morning, Yasmin walks the last part of the way to school along a busy road. At the start of the school day, the road outside Ehel Academy fills up with cars and taxis. The air smells of fumes, the traffic is slow, and crossing the road can feel a little scary. Yasmin starts to wonder: how do children in her school get to school, and could more of them walk or cycle safely, so that there are fewer cars and cleaner air?

That question becomes Yasmin's research project for this unit. As you meet each new skill, you will see exactly what Yasmin does with it. By the end, she will have real findings that she can share with her teacher and her community. You will be doing the very same thing, with a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through the unit
explainers.body:
This unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is a topic that matters both in the wider world and right where you live. You will keep returning to it, lesson after lesson, and each new skill adds another piece to it.

Here are some topics that are big all around the world and also very real in the Horn of Africa. Any of these could become your Challenge:

Your classmates will care about different things. Layla is annoyed by the litter in the schoolyard. Sami wishes there were more places to fill up a water bottle. Nadia wants more children to be able to join in sport. Any of these could grow into a strong Challenge.

You do not have to choose right now. As you work through the skills, keep a note of any topic that makes you curious, or that gives you a little 'someone should fix this' feeling. Strong curiosity and that fix-it feeling are excellent signs of a good Challenge topic.
bullets: How children travel to school, and how to make the journey safer
Traffic and the dirty air it makes in towns like Hargeisa and Mogadishu
Litter and plastic waste in our streets and schoolyards
Clean water for every family, especially in the dry season
Staying healthy, such as drinking enough water at school
Healthy food and good school meals
Making sport and play open to every child, girls and boys
Looking after wildlife, such as the sea turtles on the Berbera coast

explainers.title: So what is research?
explainers.body:
Many people think research just means typing a question into a phone and reading the first answer. Real research is more careful than that. Research means finding out about a topic or an issue in an organised way, so that you can trust what you learn and explain it to others.

When you research well, you are really learning to do three things, and this unit teaches all three:

Along the way you will also make predictions about what you think you will find, gather information by asking and watching, and then check whether your findings turned out as you expected. Notice that 'search on a phone' is only a small part of one step. Researchers also ask people, watch what happens with their own eyes, and read printed material.
bullets: Ask the right questions about your issue.
Find useful sources of information to answer them.
Record and present what you find, so it is clear and helpful.

explainers.title: Start a research journal
explainers.body:
Before you meet the first skill, start a simple habit that real researchers use: keep a research journal. This can be a notebook or a document where you record everything about your Challenge as you go. Each time you work, write the date, then jot down what you did, what you found, and what you want to do next.

A research journal helps you in three ways. It keeps your questions, sources and results in one place, so nothing gets lost. It shows how your thinking changes over time, which you will need later for Reflection. And it makes sharing your findings much easier, because the work is already there. Keep your journal beside you as you read the rest of this file.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Knowing a global issue and a local issue
explainers.body:
Research in Global Perspectives usually starts with an issue. An issue is an important subject or problem that people want to talk about and solve. Issues come in different sizes.

The most interesting Challenges are often both at once: a global issue that also shows up as a local one. That is powerful, because you can read what the wider world knows about it, and then find out what is truly happening on your own doorstep, which no book could tell you.
bullets: A global issue affects people all over the world. Dirty air in busy cities, plastic waste in the oceans and a warming climate are all global issues.
A local issue is a problem right where you live, in your own town or neighbourhood. A blocked drain on your street, or litter in your schoolyard, is a local issue.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Local, national and global questions
explainers.body:
Once you have an issue, you ask questions about it. A clever trick is to notice that questions can point at three different sizes of the world:

Strong research uses a range of questions, some local, some national, and some global. Local questions help you gather your own facts. National and global questions help you understand the bigger picture and compare your area with others. Together they give you a much fuller answer.
bullets: A local question is about your own area: your school, street or town.
A national question is about your whole country.
A global question is about the whole world.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Choosing the best sources, and giving your reasons
explainers.body:
The places your information comes from are called sources. Different questions need different sources, so a good researcher knows where to look and who to ask. It helps to split sources into two groups: people you can ask and places you can look.

People you can ask include:

Places you can look include:

A strong researcher does not just grab the first source. You choose the best source for each question, and you can give a reason for your choice. If someone asks 'why did you use that source?', you should be able to answer. That habit of giving reasons will make your research much more convincing.
bullets: Family and friends — easy to reach, and good for personal experiences.
Other students — perfect when you want to know what young people your age think or do.
Professionals — people who work with the issue, such as a nurse, a teacher or a traffic officer, who often know the most.
Books — carefully checked, and good for background facts.
Online — fast and full of information, but you must check who wrote it.
Newspapers and magazines — good for local news and recent events.
Television and radio — good for stories and interviews you can listen to.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Gathering answers with questionnaires, surveys and interviews
explainers.body:
Some of the best research is the information you gather yourself, first-hand. Three tools help you do this: a questionnaire, a survey and an interview.

Use a survey when you want numbers from many people, such as how most children travel to school. Use an interview when you want one person's fuller story, such as why one parent chooses to drive. Often the strongest research uses both: numbers from a survey, and a real story from an interview.
bullets: A questionnaire is a written set of questions you give to people.
A survey is what you are doing when you use that questionnaire with many people to find out what a lot of them think or do.
An interview is a deeper, spoken conversation with one person or a small group, to understand their views in detail.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Making predictions, and telling a prediction from a fact
explainers.body:
Before you gather your information, it is smart to make a prediction. A prediction is something you think is likely to happen, or a smart guess about what you will find. Making a prediction first gives your research a purpose: you gather information to check whether your guess was right.

Be careful not to mix up a prediction with a fact. A fact is something you can already check and show to be true. A prediction is about what you think will happen, and you cannot be sure until you find out.
bullets: Fact: More than 30 cars passed the school gate between 7:15 and 7:45 this morning. Yasmin counted them, so it can be checked.
Prediction: Most children would rather walk to school if the road felt safe. Nobody knows yet, so this is a guess to test.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Recording what you find with tally charts and tables
explainers.body:
When you gather lots of answers, you need to record them tidily, or they turn into a jumble you cannot read. Two simple tools do this beautifully: a tally chart and a table.

A tally chart lets you count as you go. Each time someone gives an answer, you make a small mark next to it. Groups of five are easy to count. A table then holds your neat totals in rows and columns, so a pattern jumps out at once.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Drawing conclusions from evidence, and how sure you can be
explainers.body:
Once your results are recorded, you draw conclusions. A conclusion is what your evidence lets you say. Evidence means the facts and results you actually gathered. The golden rule is this: you can only say what your evidence really shows, and no more. Saying more than your evidence proves is called over-claiming, and good researchers avoid it.

A helpful trick is to sort each statement into one of five levels, using only your data:
bullets: It is certainly true — the evidence clearly shows it.
It is likely to be true — the evidence points that way, but does not fully prove it.
We cannot be sure — the evidence does not tell us either way.
It is likely to be false — the evidence points against it.
It is certainly false — the evidence clearly shows it is not so.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Causes and consequences
explainers.body:
To understand an issue deeply, ask two questions about it: what are its causes, and what are its consequences? A cause is a reason the issue happens. A consequence is a result that follows from it. One often leads to the other, like dominoes falling.

Thinking about causes and consequences helps in two ways. It shows you why the problem exists, and it shows you what harm it does, which is exactly the information you need to suggest a helpful change.

explainers.title: Skill 9: Mind-maps that lead to action questions
explainers.body:
A mind-map is a quick way to get lots of ideas out of your head and onto the page. You write your topic in the middle, draw a circle around it, and then add every question you can think of around the edge. Do not stop to judge them; just get them down.

Here is the clever part. Once your mind-map is full, look for the questions that could lead to a real action for positive change, and mark each one with a star. These action questions are gold, because they point straight at something you could actually do.

explainers.title: Skill 10: Presenting your findings and deciding what to do
explainers.body:
Findings are only useful if others can understand them, so you must present them clearly. Three good ways are a tally chart, a table and a bar chart. A bar chart uses bars of different heights, so a reader can see the biggest and smallest amounts in a single glance.

How you present depends on your information and your reader. Numbers usually suit a table or a bar chart. A person's story from an interview usually suits a few careful sentences. Whatever you choose, be ready to give a reason for your choice, just as you did for your sources.

explainers.title: How research feeds the other five skills
explainers.body:
Research is the first Global Perspectives skill for a reason: it feeds all the others. Once you have researched a topic well, the rest becomes possible.

So the effort you put into research now is never wasted. It is the foundation the whole subject is built on.
bullets: Analysis needs good information before you can break a topic into causes and consequences.
Evaluation needs trustworthy sources before you can judge how strong an idea really is.
Reflection grows every time you notice how your research changed your mind.
Collaboration works better when everyone brings well-researched ideas to share.
Communication is only as strong as the research behind it, because facts make your message believable.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the research cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every research skill in this unit. Here is how they fit together into one smooth cycle you can use for any issue:
bullets: Choose an issue, and decide whether it is local, national or global, or all three.
Ask a range of good questions about it.
Choose the best sources, and give your reasons.
Make a prediction about what you think you will find.
Gather information with a questionnaire, survey, interview, or by watching.
Record your results in a tally chart or table.
Draw careful conclusions from your evidence, without over-claiming.
Present your findings clearly, in a table or a bar chart.
Decide on a fair course of action: what should happen next?

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Analysis. Once you can research a topic well, analysis teaches you to break it apart and ask, more deeply, why things happen and what the consequences are. Strong research now will make strong analysis much easier later. Well done for starting your Global Perspectives journey with a solid foundation.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a bus, and the skill is where the bus takes you.
We will use real-world topics such as traffic and clean air, litter, clean water and healthy food.
But the real prize is not to become an expert on traffic. It is to become a strong researcher who could find out about almost anything.

bigIdeas.title: The four big questions a researcher asks
lines: What questions will I ask to find out about my issue?
Who or what are the best sources of information?
How can I record and present what I find in the most helpful way?
Have I found out everything I wanted, and are my findings as I expected?

bigIdeas.title: A fairness note for Global Perspectives
lines: People often see the same issue in different ways. This point of view is called a perspective.
One family may drive because the walk feels unsafe. Another may wish there were fewer cars and cleaner air.
A good researcher listens to all these perspectives fairly, instead of only their own. Seeing an issue from many sides is at the heart of Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a good survey question
lines: It is clear, so everyone understands it the same way.
It is about your topic and your purpose, not just interesting.
It can be answered quickly, often by choosing from a short list.
It is not leading. A leading question pushes people to one answer, such as: do you agree our air is terrible? A fair question would be: how would you describe the air near our school?

bigIdeas.title: A fair question respects everyone
lines: Imagine Sami is surveying how much water children drink at school. A fair researcher remembers that families live in different ways.
During Ramadan, many Muslim children fast from food and water in the daytime. During Lent, some Christian children give up certain treats.
So Sami writes his questions and reads his results kindly, knowing that people's habits differ. Listening to everyone evenly is at the heart of Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: Sorting issues, causes and consequences
lines: Energy: burning coal to make electricity is a cause; greenhouse gases in the air is a consequence.
Food: children eating too much sugar is a cause; poor health is a consequence.
Water: too little water is the issue; families using less than they need is a consequence.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one issue that matters both in the world and where you live. This is your Challenge.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you genuinely care about.
By the end you will have real research you can share with your teacher.

bigIdeas.title: Fix a leading question
lines: A leading question pushes people to one answer, such as: do you agree our streets are far too dirty?
A fair version lets people say what they really think, such as: how clean or dirty do you find our streets?
Read each of your questions and rewrite any that push people towards an answer.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a good interview question
lines: It is open, inviting a full answer rather than just yes or no.
It is polite, clear and easy to understand.
It lets the person share their own story and their own perspective.
A useful follow-up is simply: can you tell me more about that?
Remember to be kind and respectful. Thank the person for their time, let them skip any question they do not want to answer, and never share their name without asking first.

bigIdeas.title: The bar chart in words
lines: Car: a bar reaching 11 children.
Walk: a bar reaching 4 children.
Taxi: a bar reaching 2 children.
Bus: a bar reaching 1 child. Bicycle: a bar reaching 1 child. Other: a bar reaching 1 child.

models.title: Research happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine you want to buy the best schoolbag in the market for the lowest price.
You ask a clear question: which bag lasts longest without costing too much?
You gather information: you feel the cloth, ask the seller, and ask two friends who own bags.
You think about who to trust: the seller wants a sale, so you trust your friends a little more.
Then you decide, using what you found. That is real research, and you already do it.

So research is not a strange, school-only activity. It is a careful, honest way of finding things out, and you can get better and better at it. In this unit you will simply learn to do it on purpose, with more skill, and about topics that matter to your community.

models.title: Yasmin sees a global issue on her own road
lines: Traffic and dirty air is a global issue: cities all over the world struggle with too many cars and unhealthy air.
It is also a very local issue for Yasmin: the road outside Ehel Academy is jammed and smells of fumes every morning.
Because it is both, Yasmin can learn from the wider world and also gather her own facts right outside her school.

models.title: Yasmin sorts her questions by size
lines: Local: How do the children at Ehel Academy travel to school each morning?
National: What does the law in our country say about car fumes and safe crossings?
Global: Why does heavy traffic make the air dirty in cities everywhere?
One issue, three sizes of question, and each one teaches Yasmin something different.

models.title: Yasmin matches sources to her questions, and says why
lines: To find out how children travel to school, the best source is the students themselves, because only they know how they travel. So Yasmin will ask them directly.
To learn about safe crossings and car fumes, a professional such as a road-safety officer is best, because it is their job to know.
To understand dirty air around the world, a book or a trusted website is best, because they gather facts from many places.

models.title: Yasmin designs her Travelling to School questionnaire
lines: Question 1: How do you travel to school? Car, taxi, bus, bicycle, walk, or other.
Question 2: How long does your journey take? Under 15 minutes, 15 to 30 minutes, or over 30 minutes.
Question 3: Do you ever feel unsafe on the way? Never, sometimes, or often.
Yasmin will give this questionnaire to 20 classmates as a survey, then interview one parent to learn why they drive.

models.title: Yasmin makes her prediction
lines: Yasmin's prediction: I think most children in my class come to school by car.
She also predicts a reason: I think families drive because the road feels unsafe to walk.
Now her survey has a clear purpose. When the results come in, she will check whether her predictions were right.

models.title: Yasmin records her survey in a tally table
lines: As each classmate answers, Yasmin makes a tally mark beside their type of transport.
Then she adds up each row to get a total: Car 11, Taxi 2, Bus 1, Bicycle 1, Walk 4, Other 1.
A messy list of 20 answers would tell her almost nothing. The tidy table shows at a glance that most of her class comes by car.

Recording is not just neat handwriting. A good table makes your evidence clear, so that you, your teacher and your community can all see the same pattern. Always choose a way of recording that suits the information you gathered.

models.title: Yasmin checks how sure she can be
lines: A lot of children in my class come to school by car: certainly true, because 11 of her 20 classmates said so.
A lot of children across the whole school come by car: likely to be true, because she only asked her own class, not everyone.
Children come by car because their families do not care about clean air: we cannot be sure, because her survey never asked about that.
By staying inside her evidence, Yasmin keeps her conclusions honest and strong.

models.title: Yasmin maps causes and consequences
lines: A cause: many families drive because walking on the busy road feels unsafe.
A consequence: more cars mean more fumes, so the air is harder to breathe, and the jammed road is more dangerous to cross.
Seeing this chain helps Yasmin. If she could make walking feel safe, the cause would shrink, and the consequences would ease.

models.title: Yasmin stars the action questions on her mind-map
lines: In the middle she writes: getting to school safely.
Ordinary questions: How many children come by car? How long does the walk take? Why does school start at eight?
Action questions, each with a star: Could we start a walking bus? Could families share car journeys? Could the school ask for a safe crossing?
The starred questions are the ones Yasmin will follow, because each could turn into a real improvement for her school. A mind-map turns a vague worry into a set of clear, doable next steps.

models.title: Yasmin presents her findings and chooses an action
lines: Yasmin shows her transport totals as a bar chart, because the tall Car bar makes the problem clear at a glance.
Her conclusion: most children in her class come by car, and the busy road is part of the reason.
Her course of action: suggest a walking bus for children who live nearby, and car-sharing for families who live further away, to cut the number of cars.

That last step, deciding on a sensible course of action, is what research is really for. You gather information not just to know more, but to help make something better. When your findings point to a fair, doable action, your research has done its job.

models.title: Yasmin's whole journey, from worry to action
lines: Skills 1 and 2: She turned a worry about traffic into local, national and global questions.
Skill 3: She chose the best sources and gave her reasons.
Skills 4 and 5: She made a prediction, then designed a survey and an interview.
Skill 6: She recorded her answers in a neat tally table.
Skill 7: She drew honest conclusions and did not over-claim.
Skills 8 and 9: She mapped causes and consequences, and starred her action questions.
Skill 10: She presented a bar chart and suggested a walking bus and car-sharing.

By following this cycle, Yasmin turned an everyday worry about a busy road into real, organised findings, and a fair plan she can share. In the Activities file, you will run the same cycle on your own Challenge topic, one step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you the whole way.

models.title: A model mind-map: litter in the schoolyard
lines: In the middle: litter in our schoolyard.
Branches: How much litter is dropped each day? Where does most of it end up? Why do people drop it? Are there enough bins? What could our school do? What do other students think?
Notice how these questions come from different angles, which is exactly what you want.

models.title: A model tally table: how do you travel to school?
lines: Car: five marks, total 5. Walk: four marks, total 4. Bus: two marks, total 2.
Bicycle: one mark, total 1. Other: one mark, total 1.
The tally makes counting easy, and the totals show the pattern at a glance.

models.title: A model: from causes to action
lines: Issue: litter in the schoolyard. Cause: not enough bins, and bins are far from the field.
Consequence: rubbish blows around, and the yard looks and smells unpleasant.
Action questions, each starred: Could we add bins near the field? Could each class take a turn to keep an area tidy?

models.title: A model: presenting and acting
lines: Finding: 11 of 20 children in the class come to school by car.
Best form: a bar chart, because the numbers are easy to compare and the tall Car bar stands out.
Action: my research suggests that we could start a walking bus for children who live close to school.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 1 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Research.
Ask it: In one or two simple sentences, why is research a useful skill, even outside of school?
Then tell your tutor which of the six skills you think will be the easiest for you, and which will be the hardest, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think research means.
Ask it: Is my idea missing anything important?
Then ask your tutor to give you one everyday example of research that has nothing to do with school.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one issue you care about.
Ask it to help you explain how that issue is global, affecting people around the world.
Then ask: how does the same issue show up locally, right where I live?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your issue, and try to say one local, one national and one global question about it.
Ask the tutor whether you have sorted them correctly.
Then ask it to help you improve the question that feels the weakest.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor two questions from your Challenge.
Ask it to help you choose the best source for each question: a person to ask, or a place to look.
For each one, practise giving your reason out loud: I would use this source because.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your Challenge topic and what you want to find out from people.
Ask it to help you write three or four clear questionnaire questions.
Then ask: are any of my questions leading or unclear, and how would you fix them?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one prediction about your Challenge, starting with the words I think.
Ask it whether your prediction is a real prediction or actually a fact you could already check.
Then ask the tutor how you could gather information to test whether your prediction is right.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what kind of answers you will collect, such as types of transport or yes and no answers.
Ask it to help you design a simple tally chart or table to record them.
Then ask: once my table is full, what pattern should I look for?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor one result from your research, real or imagined.
Tell it a conclusion you might draw, then ask: does my evidence really show this, or am I over-claiming?
Ask the tutor to help you reword any conclusion so that it matches exactly what your evidence shows.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your Challenge issue.
Ask it to help you name two causes of the issue and two consequences of it.
Then ask: which cause could a young researcher like me actually help to change?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your mind-map questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you spot which of your questions are action questions that could lead to real change.
Then ask the tutor to suggest one action question you did not think of.

toolkit.title: The research cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your issue, good research follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Choose an issue: decide whether it is local, national or global.
Ask questions: make a range of local, national and global questions.
Choose sources: decide who to ask and where to look, and why.
Predict: make a smart guess about what you will find.
Gather: use a questionnaire, survey, interview, or watch with your own eyes.
Record: put your results in a tally chart or table.
Conclude: say what your evidence shows, without over-claiming.
Present: show your findings in a table or a bar chart.
Act: decide on a fair course of action.

toolkit.title: The Research skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Research means finding out about a topic or an issue in an organised way, so that you can trust what you learn and explain it to someone else. It is not just typing a question into a phone. Real research means asking the right questions, choosing good sources, gathering information by asking and watching, recording it tidily, and drawing honest conclusions.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, gather your own evidence, and only say what that evidence really shows. Second, be fair, listening to different people and perspectives before you decide. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 6 Research learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your research skills grow in three stages this year. Here are the real learning goals for each stage, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

toolkit.title: Local, national or global? A quick sorter
toolkit.intro: Use a range of questions of all three sizes. Ask yourself: what part of the world is this question about?

rows: Local
My own school, street or town.
How do children at my school travel in?
National
My whole country.
What does the law say about car fumes?
Global
The whole world.
Why does traffic make city air dirty everywhere?

toolkit.title: A guide to choosing your sources
toolkit.intro: Different questions need different sources. Choose the best one for each question, and always be ready to give your reason.

rows: Family and friends
You want personal experiences and are just starting out.
What was school like when you were young?
Other students
You want to know what young people your age think or do.
How do you travel to school?
Professionals
You need expert knowledge from someone whose job it is.
How can a crossing be made safer?
Books
You want background facts that have been carefully checked.
Why is clean air important for health?
Online
You want a lot of information quickly (but check who wrote it).
Which countries make the most waste?
Newspapers and radio
You want local news, recent events or real stories.
What is happening about traffic in our town?

toolkit.title: Template: a questionnaire
toolkit.intro: Copy this template to plan a survey. Keep your questions clear, on-topic, quick to answer, and never leading. Give short answer choices where you can, so the answers are easy to count.

rows: My topic
My prediction (I think ...)
Question 1 (with answer choices)
Question 2 (with answer choices)
Question 3
Question 4
Who I will ask, and how many

toolkit.title: How sure can I be? A guide to conclusions
toolkit.intro: When you draw a conclusion, say only what your evidence shows. Sort each statement into one of these five levels, using your data alone. Saying more than the evidence proves is called over-claiming, and it makes your research weaker.

rows: Certainly true
The evidence clearly shows it.
Most children I asked come by car (11 of 20 said so).
Likely to be true
The evidence points that way, but does not fully prove it.
Most of the whole school probably comes by car.
We cannot be sure
The evidence does not tell us either way.
Families drive because they dislike walking.
Likely to be false
The evidence points against it.
Hardly anyone in my class comes by car.
Certainly false
The evidence clearly shows it is not so.
Nobody in my class comes by car.

toolkit.title: Recording and presenting: tally, table and bar chart
toolkit.intro: Always choose the form that makes your finding easiest to understand, and be ready to give a reason for your choice.
items: Tally chart: best while you are still counting. Make one mark per answer, in groups of five, then add up the totals.
Table: best for holding neat totals in rows and columns, so patterns are easy to see.
Bar chart: best for comparing amounts. Taller bars mean bigger numbers, and the biggest and smallest stand out at a glance.
A few sentences or a quotation: best for a person's story from an interview, which numbers cannot capture.

toolkit.title: Question starters for surveys and interviews
toolkit.intro:
Use these to write clear, fair questions. Keep them short and never leading.

Avoid starters like 'Don't you agree that ...?' or 'Isn't it obvious that ...?'. These are leading, because they push people towards one answer.
items: How do you usually ...?
How often do you ...?
How would you describe ...?
How far, how long, or how many ...?
What do you think about ...?
What would help you most with ...? (good for finding actions)

checklists.title: Checklist: Is this a good research question?
checklists.intro: Tick each one. If you cannot tick them all, reword your question.
items: Clear — someone else would understand exactly what I am asking.
About my issue — it really helps me find out what I want to know.
The right size — not so easy I already know the answer, and not so huge I could never finish.
Findable — I can actually gather information to answer it.
Fair — it does not push people towards one answer.

challenge.intro: Look back at the topic list in the Lesson file (how children travel to school, traffic and air, litter, clean water, staying healthy, healthy food, sport for all, wildlife). Choose one that matters in your area, or think of your own. The best Challenge is one you are genuinely curious about, because you will be living with it for the whole unit.
topics: Write your chosen issue in one sentence: 'The issue I am working on is ...'.
Write one reason you care about it.
Decide whether it is a local, a national or a global issue, or all three. Write a sentence to explain.
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...

activities.title: Mind-map your questions
activities.label: Activity 2: Mind-map your questions
activities.intro:
Before you pick a research question, you need lots of questions to choose from. A mind-map helps you get them all out of your head and onto the page.

Aim for quantity first. A messy mind-map with many questions is far more useful than a tidy one with only two.
steps: Write your issue in the middle of a page and draw a circle around it.
Around it, write as many questions about the issue as you can, at least eight. Do not judge them yet; just get them down.
Draw lines linking any questions that seem to belong together.

boxes.title: A model mind-map: litter in the schoolyard
lines: In the middle: litter in our schoolyard.
Branches: How much litter is dropped each day? Where does most of it end up? Why do people drop it? Are there enough bins? What could our school do? What do other students think?
Notice how these questions come from different angles, which is exactly what you want.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your mind-map questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: which two or three questions look the most promising, and why?
Ask the tutor to suggest one interesting question you did not think of.

activities.title: Sort your questions - local, national or global
activities.label: Activity 3: Sort your questions - local, national or global
activities.intro:
Remember that questions can point at three sizes of the world: local (your area), national (your country) and global (the whole world). Sorting your questions this way helps you cover the whole issue, not just one corner of it.

First, warm up by sorting these three questions. Write L, N or G next to each:

Now look back at your own mind-map from Activity 2. Sort your own questions into local, national and global. If you have none in one group, write a new question to fill the gap, so you end up with at least one of each size.
steps: A. How can our school get more students to recycle?
B. What is our country doing to protect rare animals?
C. Which countries make the most plastic waste?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three warm-up answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Then read your own local, national and global questions.
Ask the tutor whether your sorting is correct, and to help you improve any question that is unclear.

activities.title: Choose and justify your sources
activities.label: Activity 4: Choose and justify your sources
activities.intro:
Different questions need different sources. Remember the two groups: people you can ask (family and friends, other students, professionals) and places you can look (books, online, newspapers and magazines, television and radio).

Pick three of your best questions. For each one, choose the source you would use, and write a reason. Giving a reason is a real research skill, so practise saying 'I would use this source because ...'.

Try to use a mix. If all three of your sources are websites, swap one for a person you could ask or a book you could read. A good researcher uses more than one kind of source.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your table of questions, sources and reasons to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether each source really fits its question.
Ask the tutor: for my most important question, is there an even better source I have missed?

boxes.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your best research question and your list of sources.
Share them in your next teacher session and ask whether they are a good fit for your issue.

activities.title: Design a questionnaire
activities.label: Activity 5: Design a questionnaire
activities.intro: Now design a questionnaire you could use to survey people about your issue. A survey is how you find out what many people think or do. Good questions are clear, on-topic, quick to answer, and never leading.
steps: Write four questions for your survey.
Make at least two of them easy to count, by giving a short list of answers to choose from.
Check each question: is it clear? Is it on-topic? Could it be answered quickly? Is it fair, not leading?

boxes.title: Fix a leading question
lines: A leading question pushes people to one answer, such as: do you agree our streets are far too dirty?
A fair version lets people say what they really think, such as: how clean or dirty do you find our streets?
Read each of your questions and rewrite any that push people towards an answer.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four questionnaire questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are any of my questions leading or unclear, and how would you fix them?
Ask the tutor to help you turn one open question into one that is easy to count.

activities.title: Plan and try an interview
activities.label: Activity 6: Plan and try an interview
activities.intro: A survey gives you numbers from many people. An interview gives you the fuller story from one person, in their own words. Both are useful, and a strong researcher can do each. Here you will plan a short interview and, if you can, try it out for real.
steps: Write five interview questions about your issue. Make them open, so the person can answer with more than just yes or no.
Choose someone you could interview, such as a family member, a neighbour or a friend.
With a trusted adult's help, ask your questions and note down the most interesting things they say.
Write one thing you learned from the interview that a survey could never have told you.

boxes.title: What makes a good interview question
lines: It is open, inviting a full answer rather than just yes or no.
It is polite, clear and easy to understand.
It lets the person share their own story and their own perspective.
A useful follow-up is simply: can you tell me more about that?
Remember to be kind and respectful. Thank the person for their time, let them skip any question they do not want to answer, and never share their name without asking first.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five interview questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether any are closed questions that could be made more open.
Ask the tutor to suggest one good follow-up question you could ask during the interview.

activities.title: Make a prediction, then run a small survey and tally it
activities.label: Activity 7: Make a prediction, then run a small survey and tally it
activities.intro: This is the exciting part: gathering real information, and finding out something no book could tell you about your own community. First make a prediction, then survey a few people, then record their answers in a tally chart.
steps: Write a prediction about what you will find, starting with 'I think ...'.
With a trusted adult's help, ask your questionnaire to a few classmates, family members or neighbours.
Make a tally mark for each answer, then add up the totals.
Compare your totals with your prediction. Was your prediction right?

boxes.title: A model tally table: how do you travel to school?
lines: Car: five marks, total 5. Walk: four marks, total 4. Bus: two marks, total 2.
Bicycle: one mark, total 1. Other: one mark, total 1.
The tally makes counting easy, and the totals show the pattern at a glance.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your prediction and your tally results.
Ask it whether your results matched your prediction, and what that tells you.
Ask the tutor to help you say what you would ask next, now that you have these results.

boxes.title: A real-world step
lines: Ask your survey questions to a few people at home or in your neighbourhood, with an adult's help.
Bring your tally chart to your next teacher session and compare it with your prediction.

activities.title: Read the data in a bar chart
activities.label: Activity 8: Read the data in a bar chart
activities.intro: Researchers must be able to read data, not just collect it. Below is a bar chart described in words. It shows how 20 children in one class travel to school. Read it carefully, then answer the questions.
steps: Which way of travelling is the most common? Which is the least common?
How many more children come by car than walk?
Write one sentence saying what this bar chart shows.
Why is a bar chart easier to read than a long list of 20 answers?

boxes.title: The bar chart in words
lines: Car: a bar reaching 11 children.
Walk: a bar reaching 4 children.
Taxi: a bar reaching 2 children.
Bus: a bar reaching 1 child. Bicycle: a bar reaching 1 child. Other: a bar reaching 1 child.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check your numbers and your sentence.
Ask the tutor why a picture like a bar chart can be clearer than words for showing amounts.

activities.title: How sure can I be? Draw careful conclusions
activities.label: Activity 9: How sure can I be? Draw careful conclusions
activities.intro:
Good researchers only say what their evidence really shows. Imagine a class surveyed 20 children and most agreed with the statement: 'There are not enough bins in our schoolyard.' Using only that evidence, sort each conclusion below into one of five levels: certainly true, likely to be true, we cannot be sure, likely to be false, or certainly false.

For each one, write the level you chose and a short reason. Watch out for over-claiming, which means saying more than your evidence proves.
steps: A lot of the children who were asked think there are not enough bins.
A lot of the teachers also think there are not enough bins.
Children drop litter only because they do not care about the schoolyard.
Not a single child in the whole school thinks there are enough bins.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers and reasons to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you have over-claimed anywhere, by saying more than the evidence shows.
Ask the tutor to help you reword any conclusion so it matches the evidence exactly.

activities.title: Sort causes and consequences, then find action questions
activities.label: Activity 10: Sort causes and consequences, then find action questions
activities.intro:
Every issue has causes (reasons it happens) and consequences (results that follow). Understanding both helps you find good actions.

First, warm up. For your issue, write two causes and two consequences in a simple two-column list.
steps: Cause 1 and Cause 2: two reasons your issue happens.
Consequence 1 and Consequence 2: two results that follow from it.
Now build a small mind-map and add questions that could lead to real change. Mark each of these action questions with a star.

boxes.title: A model: from causes to action
lines: Issue: litter in the schoolyard. Cause: not enough bins, and bins are far from the field.
Consequence: rubbish blows around, and the yard looks and smells unpleasant.
Action questions, each starred: Could we add bins near the field? Could each class take a turn to keep an area tidy?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your causes, consequences and starred action questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your action questions really point to something that could be done.
Ask the tutor to suggest one more action question for your issue.

activities.title: Present your findings and suggest an action
activities.label: Activity 11: Present your findings and suggest an action
activities.intro: Findings are only useful if others can understand them. Choose the clearest way to present what you have found, then use it to suggest a fair course of action.
steps: Write your main findings so far, in short bullet points.
Choose the best way to present them: a table, a bar chart, or a few short sentences. Write one reason for your choice.
Make a first draft of your chosen form.
Write one sensible action your findings suggest, starting with 'My research suggests that we could ...'.

boxes.title: A model: presenting and acting
lines: Finding: 11 of 20 children in the class come to school by car.
Best form: a bar chart, because the numbers are easy to compare and the tall Car bar stands out.
Action: my research suggests that we could start a walking bus for children who live close to school.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what you found and who your audience is.
Ask it whether a table or a bar chart would be clearer for your information, and why.
Ask the tutor to check that your suggested action is fair and could really be done.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'research' mean?
practice.answer: Research means finding out about a topic or issue in an organised way, so you can trust what you learn and explain it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: An issue that affects people all over the world is called a ______ issue.
practice.answer: Global.

practice.prompt: A question about your own town or school is a ______ question; a question about your whole country is a ______ question.
practice.answer: Local; national.

practice.prompt: Name one person you could ask and one place you could look for information.
practice.answer: Any one person (family or friend, another student, a professional) and any one place (book, online, newspaper or magazine, television or radio).

practice.prompt: True or false: 'Do you agree our air is terrible?' is a fair survey question.
practice.answer: False. It is leading, because it pushes people to agree the air is terrible.

practice.prompt: A question that pushes someone towards one answer is called a ______ question.
practice.answer: A leading question.

practice.prompt: What is a prediction?
practice.answer: A prediction is something you think is likely to happen, or a smart guess about what you will find, which your research then tests.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a fact, not a prediction? (a) I think most children walk to school (b) 12 children in my class walk to school (c) walking will become more popular next year.
practice.answer: (b) 12 children in my class walk to school. It can be checked, so it is a fact.

practice.prompt: What is a tally chart used for?
practice.answer: A tally chart is used to count answers as you gather them, using marks that are easy to add up.

practice.prompt: A picture that shows amounts as bars of different heights is called a ______.
practice.answer: A bar chart.

practice.prompt: If you only surveyed your own class, can you be sure the whole school thinks the same? Explain in one sentence.
practice.answer: No. You only asked your class, so you cannot be sure the rest of the school thinks the same. (This idea is the correct answer.)

practice.prompt: Saying more than your evidence proves is called ______.
practice.answer: Over-claiming.

practice.prompt: Give one cause and one consequence of traffic in a busy town.
practice.answer: Any sensible pair, such as: cause, too many cars on the road; consequence, dirty air that is hard to breathe.

practice.prompt: On a mind-map, why do we put a star next to some questions?
practice.answer: We star the questions that could lead to a real action for positive change (action questions).

practice.prompt: Give one reason why a researcher should be able to explain why they chose a source.
practice.answer: Any one of: it shows your research is careful; it helps others trust your work; it proves the source really fits the question.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each research word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Source
options: A. A smart guess about what you will find, which your research then tests.
B. A place your information comes from, such as a person, book or website.
C. A result that follows from an issue or a cause.
D. What your evidence lets you say at the end.
E. The facts and results you have gathered.
F. A picture that shows amounts as bars of different heights.
practice.answer: B — A place your information comes from, such as a person, book or website.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Prediction
practice.answer: A — A smart guess about what you will find, which your research then tests.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Evidence
practice.answer: E — The facts and results you have gathered.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Consequence
practice.answer: C — A result that follows from an issue or a cause.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Bar chart
practice.answer: F — A picture that shows amounts as bars of different heights.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Conclusion
practice.answer: D — What your evidence lets you say at the end.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Leila wants to know how many children in her class drink enough water. Which tool should she use to find out from many of them: a survey or an interview? Why?
practice.answer: A survey, because she wants numbers from many children, and a survey collects the same question from a lot of people quickly.

practice.prompt: Omar counted 30 cars passing the school gate in ten minutes. Is that a fact or a prediction? Explain.
practice.answer: A fact. Omar counted the cars, so it can be checked and shown to be true.

practice.prompt: Nadia surveyed her own class and found most enjoy sport. She wrote: 'Every child in the school enjoys sport.' What mistake has she made, and how should she fix it?
practice.answer: She has over-claimed, because she only asked her own class, not the whole school. She should write: most children in my class enjoy sport.

practice.prompt: Idris wants to know why families drive their children to school. Which source would help most: a book about the whole world, or an interview with a local parent? Why?
practice.answer: An interview with a local parent, because only they can tell you their own reasons, which no worldwide book would know.

practice.prompt: Sami found two causes of litter and two consequences. What should he do next to turn this into a plan of action?
practice.answer: He should turn his causes and consequences into a mind-map, star the questions that could lead to a real action, and suggest one fair change.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Working with my AI tutor, my discussion partner ...
Working with my teacher in live sessions ...
Asking a family member or neighbour ...
Writing my ideas down in my research journal as I went ...

vocabulary.meaning: A sensible step you suggest to help make an issue better.
A picture that shows amounts as bars of different heights.
The reasons that an issue or a problem happens.
What your evidence lets you say at the end of your research.
The results that follow from an issue or a cause.
The facts and results you have gathered to support an idea.
The facts and details you find out about your issue.
Spoken conversations with one person or a small group to learn their views.
The whole job of finding out about an issue, from question to conclusion.
An important subject or problem that people want to discuss and solve.
An issue that affects people all over the world.
An issue right where you live, in your own area.
Smart guesses about what you think you will find, which you then test.
A written set of questions you give to people in a survey.
Using a questionnaire with many people to find out what they think or do.
The answers and totals you get after gathering your information.
The people you ask and the places you look for information.
A chart where you make a mark for each answer to count them easily.
Rows and columns that hold your neat totals so patterns are clear.
Saying more than your evidence proves; something good researchers avoid.
The point of view someone has, shaped by who they are and where they live.
The fair, sensible plan you suggest once your research is done.

mistakes: Asking a question that is too easy, too huge, or unclear.
Using only one source, or only sources that agree with you.
Writing a leading question that pushes people towards one answer.
Recording answers in a messy jumble instead of a tally chart or table.
Over-claiming, by saying more than your evidence really shows.
Collecting lots of information but never presenting it clearly.
Forgetting to turn your findings into a fair course of action.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'research' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Research means finding out about a topic or issue in an organised way, so you can trust what you learn and explain it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: An issue that affects people all over the world is called a ______ issue.
A question about your own town or school is a ______ question; a question about your whole country is a ______ question.
Name one person you could ask and one place you could look for information.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one person (family or friend, another student, a professional) and any one place (book, online, newspaper or magazine, television or radio).

questions.prompt: True or false: 'Do you agree our air is terrible?' is a fair survey question.
questions.modelAnswer: False. It is leading, because it pushes people to agree the air is terrible.

questions.prompt: A question that pushes someone towards one answer is called a ______ question.

questions.modelAnswer: A prediction is something you think is likely to happen, or a smart guess about what you will find, which your research then tests.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a fact, not a prediction? (a) I think most children walk to school (b) 12 children in my class walk to school (c) walking will become more popular next year.
questions.modelAnswer: (b) 12 children in my class walk to school. It can be checked, so it is a fact.

questions.prompt: What is a tally chart used for?
questions.modelAnswer: A tally chart is used to count answers as you gather them, using marks that are easy to add up.

questions.prompt: A picture that shows amounts as bars of different heights is called a ______.
If you only surveyed your own class, can you be sure the whole school thinks the same? Explain in one sentence.
questions.modelAnswer: No. You only asked your class, so you cannot be sure the rest of the school thinks the same. (This idea is the correct answer.)

questions.prompt: Saying more than your evidence proves is called ______.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what a global issue and a local issue are.
I can sort questions into local, national and global.
I can make my own questions to understand an issue.
I can recognise different sources and choose a good one.
I can design a questionnaire to use in a survey.
I can make a prediction about what I will find.
I can record my results in a tally chart or table.
I can read a tally chart or bar chart and answer questions about it.
I can draw conclusions from evidence without over-claiming.
I can name causes and consequences of an issue.
I can give reasons for choosing a source or a way of presenting.
I can use my results to suggest a course of action.
